terms.definition: An empty intersection next to a stone along a board line; diagonal points do not count.
A connected group has only one liberty left and may be captured next.
When a move removes the opponent group's final liberty, the group is taken off the board.
Play next to your own group along a line, connecting the new stone and then recounting the group's liberties.
Stones of one colour connected along board lines. Diagonal contact alone does not join groups.
An empty point touching two of your groups that can join them with a legal move.
An empty point where the opponent could directly connect two groups; occupying it blocks that particular connection.
A move that leaves your group without liberties and captures nothing.
Under the simple-ko rule you may not immediately retake a stone if it recreates the preceding position.
A meaningful threat elsewhere intended to draw a reply before contesting a ko again.
An enclosed empty point or region inside a group.
An eye the opponent cannot safely occupy; two separate real eyes generally let a group live in these basic positions.
A space that resembles an eye but can still be entered or destroyed by the opponent.
A point that can significantly change eyes, liberties or connections.
The early phase of a game, when moves establish useful space and relationships between groups.
The phase when groups interact more closely and fighting, security and life-and-death questions become more important.
The later phase in which players settle remaining boundaries and compare local point gains after major groups are relatively safe.
A group whose connection, liberties, eyes or escape routes are not yet secure and which may face attack.
The standard full-sized Go board has 19 lines each way and 361 intersections. This small diagram illustrates direction, not the whole board.
Planning early moves across the board, often using corners and sides while considering how nearby stones work together.
Where a move develops in relation to neighbouring groups, space and support, rather than a coordinate to memorise.
An area with sufficiently settled boundaries that ownership is relatively clear; its value still follows the chosen scoring rules.
A solid, relatively safe formation that can support nearby fighting or development; it is not automatically worth a fixed number of points.
The potential of a position to affect nearby or central play beyond its immediate territory; potential is not guaranteed points.
A group that can be pressured because its eyes, liberties, connections or escape routes are insufficient.
A group that is comparatively secure, so an opponent cannot easily turn a short attack into a severe life-and-death threat.
Playing against a weaker group to gain strength, territory or initiative; capturing every opposing stone is not required.
Considering moves and the opponent's strongest replies in sequence to test whether a group can live or be captured.
The opposing move that most seriously challenges your intended continuation in the local position.
An intersection that can make a decisive difference to eye space, liberties or connections.
Whose turn it is in the position; this can change the result and is different from sente as an initiative concept.
The stage of settling remaining boundaries and comparing local gains after most large groups are reasonably secure.
A unit used here for a local score or score difference. Whole-board scoring depends on the rules in use.
The initiative retained when a move usually demands an answer and you may be able to play first elsewhere afterwards; it is not guaranteed.
A move that prevents immediate serious loss, such as a group dying or a major invasion, and may matter more than a larger ordinary endgame move.
Comparing weak groups, unsettled spaces and support across the board before deciding where to play next.
An area where failing to respond promptly may cause a major and near-term loss.
A promising open area offering substantial value but not necessarily posing immediate danger.
Deliberately accepting the loss of a few stones in return for benefits elsewhere on the board.
The outside strength, territory, attacking chances or initiative obtained in exchange for giving up stones.
The reach and usefulness of stones toward the centre or another area; it is not already secured territory.
The opportunity to retain the move and reach the next important area first after a move that normally calls for an answer.
A move elsewhere that the opponent has a strong reason to answer while you prepare to contest a ko again.
The difference between winning and losing the ko in the full position; it helps determine how much to spend on threats.
The exchange of threats and responses while both players contest the right to retake a ko point.
A commonly studied sequence of reasonable corner exchanges under particular conditions; never a context-free guarantee of the best move.
The useful strength and reach toward the rest of the board arising from a local exchange.
Choosing which way a local variation develops in relation to friendly support, opposing strength and whole-board needs.
Revisiting a completed game to examine key decisions, recover your original reasoning and choose a question to test next time.
A position where a decision significantly changed the result or the safety of an important group.
An alternative move worth comparing in the same position, not necessarily the only correct or best move.
The move recorded as actually played in the game; it is a historical baseline, not automatically the uniquely best move.

sourceSemantics: Glossary terms only; demonstration captions have one source of truth at locales/en/core-demo-drafts.json. Neither copy is allowed to change item rules or scoring.
